strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework using statistical physics tools (MSRDJ formalism, VGA) with sound self-averaging argument and CLT justification for Gaussianity
Novel unification of Bayesian inference, gradient flow, and Langevin dynamics in single theoretical framework
Parsimonious description using two order parameters (R̄ and C̄), more interpretable than prior work requiring auxiliary fields
Insightful mechanistic explanation of early stopping via bias-variance decomposition and analysis of regularization effects on variance vs. bias timescales
Strong experimental validation across Figures 1-4 with systematic parameter variation (β, gβ, γ) and adequate disorder averaging (10⁵ realizations)
Elegant mathematical development reducing high-dimensional dynamics to interpretable lower-dimensional order parameters with memory kernel mediating mode coupling
Thorough technical exposition with detailed appendices (A-E) providing complete derivations from disorder averaging to effective equations
weaknesses: Severely limited applicability: restricted to linear/kernel regression without feature learning; connection to real neural networks is indirect and unproven

Power-law eigenvalue spectrum assumed as input (Eq. 9) rather than derived from architecture or data; claim to 'explain' neural scaling laws (p. 1) is overstated—theory explains dynamics *given* power laws, not their origin
Large-N asymptotic analysis throughout with no finite-size corrections or breakdown analysis; unclear how accurate theory is for N≈100-1000 tested in simulations
Strong assumptions (Gaussian features, orthogonality relation) with limited robustness analysis; no exploration of failures under non-Gaussian or correlated features
Incomplete quantitative characterization of early stopping: no analytical formula for optimal stopping time t_opt(β, gβ, γ, P, N) or explicit time-dependent scaling laws L_test(t)
Experiments limited to synthetic data with modest system sizes; main power-law exponent tested only at γ=3/2; no real-data validation or regime where theory fails
Presentation density with heavy notation (bars, tildes, hats) and key intuitions (memory kernel as Onsager term) relegated to Discussion; physical interpretation could precede mathematics

strengths: Technically rigorous framework using sophisticated statistical physics tools (MSRDJ formalism, variational Gaussian approximation) that appears mathematically sound
Successfully unifies multiple learning scenarios (Bayesian inference, gradient flow with/without weight decay, Langevin dynamics) in a single framework
Provides quantitative bias-variance decomposition showing how bias decays monotonically while variance accumulates, offering insight into early stopping dynamics
Strong theory-experiment agreement demonstrated across different eigenmode indices, noise levels, and regularization strengths
Elegant reduction of high-dimensional microscopic behavior to interpretable order parameters through mean-field analysis
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily applies established statistical physics techniques to a specific case; improvements over Bordelon et al. (2025) and Canatar et al. (2021) are incremental (L2 regularization, fewer order parameters, inclusion of Langevin dynamics)
Severely restricted to kernel regression regime; entirely restricted to linearized networks with no extension to feature learning in nonlinear networks, limiting practical relevance

Misleading framing of 'neural scaling laws': actual neural scaling laws involve complex interactions between model size, data size, architecture; this work delivers kernel regression analysis only, not explanation of actual neural scaling phenomena
No validation on real data or actual neural networks; all experiments use synthetic data with exactly the assumed feature distributions and power laws

Questionable fundamental assumptions not thoroughly validated: Gaussian features assumed without robustness analysis; power-law exponent γ fixed at 3/2 across all experiments with no sensitivity analysis; teacher-student setup is artificial

Incomplete technical analysis: VGA approximation claimed 'exact' in large N limit but validity for finite N (experiments use N=100) not analyzed; truncation of series in Appendix B not fully justified; self-consistent equations require numerical solution with sparse implementation details

Unclear actionable insights: early stopping via bias-variance tradeoff is well-established since Krogh & Hertz (1992); spectral bias largely reiterates Canatar et al. (2021); no new algorithmic or architectural principles
Missing exploration of parameter space: limited ablations, mostly fixed γ=3/2 and P=N, no investigation of other overparameterization regimes or sensitivity to hyperparameters
No code provided and sparse implementation details for solving self-consistent equations; reproducibility concerns
Missing related work on double descent, scaling laws beyond kernel regime, and implicit regularization in modern neural networks

strengths: Technically solid mathematical framework using MSRDJ formalism with detailed, reproducible derivations in appendices
Unifying perspective elegantly combining Bayesian inference, gradient flow, and Langevin dynamics within single theoretical framework using only two order parameters
Well-motivated focus on power-law distributed spectra, which are ubiquitous in real data
Insightful physical interpretation: response function K as Onsager reaction term, clear bias-variance decomposition explaining early stopping mechanisms
Strong quantitative theory-simulation agreement across multiple parameter regimes (Figures 1-4)
Nuanced analysis of regularization effects showing differential impact on fast vs. slow modes through Green's functions
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: theory applies only to linear/kernel regression, not neural networks, despite title emphasizing 'neural scaling laws'—connection between NTK and present results unclear; feature learning absent

Restrictive and incompletely justified assumptions: orthogonality (Eq. 8) doesn't hold exactly for finite data; Gaussian features assumption ψ_i ~ N(0, η_i δ_{ij}) is specific; exact power-law decay η_i = η_1 i^{-1-γ} is idealized—none empirically validated

No real-data experiments: all validation uses synthetic data perfectly matching model assumptions; despite motivation citing image/language data with power-law spectra, no experiments on realistic datasets; system sizes (N, P ≤ 10^4) are small

Incomplete novelty assessment: main contribution combines existing techniques (MSRDJ, VGA from prior work) with power-law spectra; Bordelon et al. (2025) already studied power-law dynamics; early stopping via bias-variance is well-known (Krogh & Hertz 1992); paper explains mechanism but doesn't discover fundamentally new phenomena

Theoretical justification gaps: claim that VGA becomes exact in large N limit via central limit theorem is hand-wavy (CLT requires specific mean-field scaling; complex interdependencies through Q); self-consistency equations' existence/uniqueness/stability not proven; self-averaging assumption not rigorously validated; no finite-N error bounds provided

Very dense presentation with steep learning curve: jumps from setup to advanced MSRDJ formalism without intuition; notation introduced without definition; physical meaning of order parameters unclear before equations introduced

Incomplete analysis: relationship between β, γ, and optimal stopping time mentioned but not explored; Figure 4 on regularization effects lacks detailed interpretation; 'disorder-induced effective self-coupling' lacks clear articulation of novelty

Limited comparison with most closely related work (Bordelon et al. 2025): paper claims fewer/more interpretable order parameters but provides no quantitative comparison, ablation studies, or demonstration of advantages

Missing validation on realistic settings: no demonstration that theoretical insights transfer to real neural networks; unclear practical impact of precise predictions vs. qualitative insights; no sensitivity analysis of chosen hyperparameters (β, g, N, P)

strengths: Rigorous and comprehensive dynamical mean-field theory using MSRDJ formalism and variational Gaussian approximation, properly handling disorder averaging and recovering known limits as validation
Successfully unifies multiple learning regimes (Bayesian inference, gradient flow, Langevin dynamics) under a single theoretical framework with interpretable order parameters (R, C, C̃)

Novel mechanistic insights including: memory kernel mediating mode coupling and learning slowdown, mode decoupling conditional on order parameters, bias-variance decomposition explaining early stopping, and the striking result that optimal stopping time is independent of P and N
Thorough experimental validation with good theory-simulation agreement across multiple parameter regimes and extensions (label noise, different regularization strengths)

Exceptionally detailed mathematical exposition in appendices (A-C) that makes derivations transparent and reproducible, with careful identification of order parameters and justification for dropping subleading terms
weaknesses: Severely restricted scope: limited entirely to linear kernel regression. No results for feature learning or nonlinear networks beyond brief speculative discussion. Applicability to understanding real neural networks remains unclear, undermining stated motivation

Critical unjustified assumptions: (1) Gaussian features ψᵢ~N(0,ηᵢδᵢⱼ)—robustness to non-Gaussian or structured kernels unknown; (2) specific power-law decay ηᵢ=η₁i^{-1-γ}—no guidance on identifying α from data; (3) identical student-teacher features—artificial relative to prior work on down-projected settings; (4) VGA exactness only as N→∞—finite-N convergence rates not characterized

Presentation issues: extremely dense notation with scattered key results across appendices limits accessibility. Figures 2b and 3 are difficult to parse. The intuitive interpretation of scaling laws (Section 5) lacks intermediate explanation connecting microscopic dynamics to macroscopic phenomena

Limited technical novelty in some components: scaling laws (Eqs. 34-37) recover Bordelon et al. (2024) as acknowledged; static limit recovers Canatar et al. (2021) exactly; label noise extension is straightforward application of framework

Approximations lack rigor: (1) OUP approximation (replacing Q with ⟨Q⟩) provides lower bound on bias decay with unanalyzed tightness; (2) finite-size corrections O(N^{-α}) can be substantial (visible in figures) but not thoroughly analyzed; (3) self-averaging property stated but not proven with finite-N rates

Limited experimental scope and practical utility: modest system sizes (N,P≤1000), only one or two power-law exponents tested, visible theory-simulation discrepancies at intermediate times, no demonstration on realistic datasets or guidance on estimating α from data, unclear how to apply results for algorithm design

Missing critical analyses: no robustness study for violations of Gaussian assumption, no characterization of convergence to mean-field limit, no discussion of phase transitions when Pηᵢ~1/gβ, limited treatment of how results change with input correlations or non-isotropic features

strengths: Unified framework successfully integrating Bayesian inference, gradient flow, and Langevin dynamics under a single theory
Technically rigorous mean-field derivations with comprehensive appendices
Novel mechanistic insights including effective memory kernels and temporally correlated noise characterization
Clear explanation of early stopping through bias-variance decomposition (Figure 2b)
Explicit power-law scaling laws relating spectrum, regularization, and optimal stopping time
Good empirical validation within the linear setting across multiple parameter regimes
weaknesses: Fundamental scope limitation: theory applies only to linear regression, yet paper frames contribution as addressing neural scaling laws and neural networks—the NNGP connection is speculative and unsupported
Restrictive assumptions poorly satisfied by real data: Gaussian features, exact power-law spectra, orthogonal covariance, simultaneous N→∞ and P,t→∞ limits
Incomplete theoretical justification: VGA approximation quality not quantified; Gaussian approximation proof is somewhat circular; sum-to-integral conversions lack rigor

Scaling law analysis contradictory: Section 5 uses OUP bound that 'neglects fluctuations of Q' despite disorder coupling being central to the theory; N^{-α} corrections acknowledged as non-negligible but dismissed
Early stopping result (Eq. 36) emerges from OUP bound, not full theory; independence from P,N is striking but lacks rigorous proof
No validation on realistic data; all experiments use synthetic Gaussian features on small systems (N,P≤1000); disorder averaging over 10⁵ realizations unrepresentative of actual learning
Limited methodological novelty: MSRDJ and VGA are from prior work (Helias & Dahmen 2020); application to power-law spectra is incremental
Significant theory-practice gap: finite-size effects important in practice but not characterized; unclear which insights transfer to networks with feature learning or finite width
Presentation issues: critical limitation to linear models relegated to Section 6; key insights obscured by mathematical density; misleading framing regarding neural networks
Reproducibility concerns: no code provided; insufficient simulation details; self-averaging assumption stated but not proven rigorously

strengths: Rigorous mathematical framework using MSRDJ formalism and variational Gaussian approximation with careful large-N analysis
Successful unification of multiple training regimes (Bayesian inference, gradient flow, Langevin dynamics) under single theoretical framework
Excellent quantitative agreement between theory and simulations across diverse regimes (Figures 1-5)
Multiple novel physical insights: spectral bias as dynamic phenomenon, disorder-induced memory kernel slowing learning, emergent noise correlations, independence of optimal stopping time from P and N
Effective reduction of high-dimensional dynamics to interpretable lower-dimensional order parameters
Comprehensive treatment including extensions to label noise and sketches toward nonlinear settings
Well-organized presentation with detailed derivations enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Restriction to linearized kernel regression and linear regression limits applicability; connection to actual neural network training through NTK is indirect
Strong assumptions on data: Gaussian feature distribution, orthogonal features with power-law decay may not generalize to broader settings
Finite-size corrections are non-negligible (Figure 4 shows N^{-α} terms), limiting practical applicability for realistic system sizes
VGA is exact only in N→∞ limit without quantified convergence analysis; Ornstein-Uhlenbeck approximation impacts not fully explored
Early stopping time result (t* independent of P, N) holds only to leading order; robustness to assumption violations not thoroughly discussed
Nonlinear extensions incomplete: Section J left for future work, no discussion of activation function dependence
Limited practical guidance: optimal stopping formula elegant but hyperparameter selection strategy unclear
Theory-experiment differences not quantified (e.g., errors as function of N, P)
Comparative advantages over closely related work (Bordelon et al. 2024) remain somewhat subtle; specific novelty could be better highlighted
